query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, high‐temperature stable, oxygen‐impermeable coating, such as an alumina-based oxide or oxide/nitride composite deposited by chemical vapor deposition or pack cementation, on the as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy will significantly enhance its oxidation resistance at 1000 °C in air while preserving its intrinsic room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C (strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1)
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin (approximately 1–5 µm) high-temperature stable oxide or oxide/nitride composite coating (e.g., alumina-based) onto the alloy surface by chemical vapor deposition or pack cementation.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 1000 °C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere (e.g., air) for up to 150 hours with mechanical testing under strain rates between 10−4 and 10−2 s−1.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, adherent coating that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, preventing surface oxidation without altering the bulk microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The coating limits oxygen ingress by forming a protective layer, thereby preventing the formation of deleterious oxides at high temperatures while maintaining the alloy's microstructural integrity and its associated mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will display a significantly lower oxidation rate (thinner oxide scale and reduced weight gain) during high-temperature exposure while retaining comparable room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength relative to the uncoated, as-cast alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr suffers from rapid oxidation under high-temperature, oxygen-containing environments, which degrades its surface integrity without affecting the bulk mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is designed for high-temperature oxidation conditions at approximately 1000 °C in air with exposure times around 150 hours, under mechanical loading conditions corresponding to strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating thickness, exact chemical composition of the protective layer, and long-term cyclic oxidation behavior remain to be fully determined to ensure no adverse interfacial reactions or embrittlement occur.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set is left untreated and the other receives the thin, high-temperature stable coating via CVD (or pack cementation). Expose both sets to air at 1000 °C for 150 hours, then perform standardized oxidation tests (measuring oxide-scale thickness and weight gain) as well as mechanical tests (room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength measured at strain rates between 10−4 and 10−2 s−1).
measurements: High-temperature yield strength at 1000 °C (mechanical testing at specified strain rates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the coated samples fail to show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation indicators (oxide scale thickness and weight gain) compared to untreated samples, or if the coating adversely affects the measured ductility and yield strength relative to the as-cast baseline.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties

decision.trend: Earlier studies on refractory high‐entropy alloys, including those based on Hf-containing systems, have largely focused on adjusting the bulk microstructure via processing routes (casting, HIP, SPS, directional solidification) and small compositional modifications (e.g., minor Cr addition) to boost strength and ductility. A few works have also noted the presence and effects of oxygen—in some cases forming oxide precipitates (as in a TiO phase) or oxygen complexes—yet these interventions were aimed at overall mechanical performance rather than specifically targeting high-temperature oxidation resistance. As a result, while impressive gains in strength and ductility have been achieved by bulk treatments, the selective control of oxygen attack in the as-cast state remains an unaddressed limitation.
decision.unsolved: There is no single, targeted intervention that directly prevents oxygen ingress and high-temperature oxidation in as‐cast HfNbTaTiZr without altering its beneficial microstructure and mechanical properties. The challenge is to improve surface oxidation resistance while maintaining the alloy’s intrinsic room‐temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength under service conditions.
decision.lever: apply a thin, high-temperature stable, oxygen-impermeable coating (for example, via chemical vapor deposition or pack cementation to form a dense oxide/nitride layer) on the as‐cast alloy surface
decision.why: Surface treatment directly targets the oxygen resistance issue by forming an external barrier that prevents oxygen ingress during high-temperature exposure. This approach avoids perturbing the bulk microstructure—thus preserving the alloy’s ductility and yield strength—and follows logically from the trend that, while bulk processing routes have been exhaustively optimized, the oxygen degradation problem remains to be solved by addressing the alloy–environment interface.
